items.title: SS2/21: Outsourcing and third party risk management (November 2024 update)
items.publisher: Bank of England, Prudential Regulation Authority
items.locator: Paras 2.4-2.6 (non-outsourcing third party arrangements, including off-the-shelf machine learning models), 4.3 (board accountability), 5.15-5.17 (due diligence), 8.3-8.4 (access, audit and information rights), 10.1 and 10.19 (exit plans)
items.quote: Firms that enter into outsourcing arrangements remain fully accountable for complying with all their regulatory obligations.
items.why: Source of the brief's quotation. The regulator's statement of what a buyer of a third-party service keeps: full accountability, due diligence on all third party arrangements and, for material outsourcing, audit rights in the contract and a documented, tested exit strategy. Buying an off-the-shelf machine learning model is given as an example of a third party arrangement that is not outsourcing: the detailed outsourcing requirements do not apply, but its materiality and risk must still be assessed. Applies to PRA-regulated banks and insurers only; a benchmark elsewhere, not a rule. Version in force (published 15 November 2024, effective 31 December 2024); a version published 18 March 2026 takes effect 18 March 2027, with paragraph 4.3 unchanged.

items.title: Artificial intelligence in UK financial services - 2024
items.publisher: Bank of England and Financial Conduct Authority
items.locator: Section 2.8 (third-party implementation, Chart 9); executive summary ('Third-party exposure'); section 1.2 (118 responses)
items.quote: The business areas with the highest percentages of third-party implementations were human resources (65%), risk and compliance (64%), and operations and IT (56%).
items.why: Source of the figure. Third-party implementations were most common in human resources (65%), risk and compliance (64%) and operations and IT (56%); across all areas they were a third of use cases, against 17% in the 2022 survey. 46% of firms reported only partial understanding of the AI they use, largely because of third-party models. Financial services only; 118 firms responded. The overall one-third figure is used by another brief, so this brief leads with the business-area split.

items.title: Procurement Act 2023, section 52: Key performance indicators
items.locator: s.52(1)-(4), (6); commencement note I2 (in force 24 February 2025). Read with s.71(2) (assessment at least once in every twelve months; in force 1 January 2026 for specified purposes)
items.quote: must set at least three key performance indicators in respect of the contract
items.why: The binding rule for public buyers on tracking a supplier through the life of a contract. Before entering a public contract with an estimated value above £5 million, a contracting authority must set and publish at least three key performance indicators, unless performance could not appropriately be assessed that way; frameworks, concession contracts and light touch contracts are excluded. Not specific to AI. Section 71, read alongside, requires assessment against them at least every twelve months and publication when a supplier fails to perform.

items.title: Supply chain security guidance: III. Check your arrangements
items.locator: Principle 10 ('Build assurance activities into your supply chain management'); page shows 'Reviewed 22 October 2025'
items.quote: Build the 'right to audit' into all contracts and exercise this.
items.why: The national technical authority's general supply chain principle on assurance: contractual upward reporting, a right to audit that is used, and key performance indicators. Notes that an audit right may not always be possible for cloud services. Not written for AI; it is the security baseline an AI supplier check sits on.

items.title: Code of Practice for the Cyber Security of AI
items.publisher: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
items.locator: Principle 7 ('Secure your supply chain'), provisions 7.1-7.4
items.quote: Developers and System Operators shall re-run evaluations on released models that they intend on using.
items.why: A voluntary government code. Principle 7 says an operator that uses a model or component that is not well documented must be able to justify the decision in writing and assess the risk, must re-run evaluations on released models it intends to use, and must tell end-users before a model is updated. Supports reassessment on change.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence Playbook for the UK Government
items.locator: Principle 8 ('You work with commercial colleagues from the start'); section 'Buying AI' ('Specifying your requirements', 'Aligning procurement and ethics')
items.quote: the same between AI systems developed in-house and those procured from a third party
items.why: Government's current guidance to its own buyers: expectations on responsible and ethical use should be the same for bought and built systems, and contracts can require transparency from the supplier. Lists what to cover when drafting requirements, including the supplier's AI approach, vendor lock-in, support and liabilities. Written for the public sector.

items.title: Data protection audit framework, Artificial intelligence toolkit: Contracts and third parties
items.locator: Second control measure (due diligence before procuring) and third control measure (written contracts)
items.quote: Before procuring AI systems, datasets or coding, there has been appropriate due diligence undertaken on accuracy, bias and the trade-offs
items.why: What the data protection regulator's auditors look for: due diligence on accuracy and bias before purchase, accuracy-based performance indicators in the contract, documentation from the developer, a timeline to re-evaluate, and regular review of outsourced services. The page carries a banner that, because of the Data (Use and Access) Act, the guidance is under review. Page metadata date 20 November 2024; no date is printed.

items.title: A pro-innovation approach to AI regulation: government response
items.publisher: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
items.locator: Section 5.2, paragraph 66 and Case study 1 ('Liability as a barrier to AI adoption in the UK'); footnote 76
items.quote: It’s common for the law to allocate liability to the last actor in the chain
items.why: The government's own statement of where liability tends to fall when a bought AI tool discriminates: on the deploying organisation, with the supplier reached only in limited circumstances (agency under equality law, contract, or negligence). A fictional case study, not a ruling, and published by the previous government; no later statement was found.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework (AI RMF 1.0), NIST AI 100-1
items.publisher: National Institute of Standards and Technology
items.locator: Table 1, GOVERN 6, 6.1 and 6.2 (document page 24; page 29 of the PDF)
items.quote: Contingency processes are in place to handle failures or incidents in third-party data or AI systems deemed to be high-risk.
items.why: International comparator. A voluntary United States framework that treats third-party software, data and supply chain as a governance category of its own: policies for third-party risk and contingency processes for third-party failure. Matches the criterion's top level (exit plans for critical dependencies).

items.title: Guidelines for AI procurement
items.locator: Top 10 considerations, items 8 and 10; section 4 ('Contract Implementation and Ongoing management')
items.quote: Consider during AI procurement that lifespan testing, not a one-time decision, is required.
items.why: The older government guidance that the 2025 Playbook still points buyers to. Used here for through-life management: monitoring the model after deployment, knowledge transfer, avoiding lock-in and black box systems, and considering independent audits. Published in 2020 and not updated since.

items.title: UK GDPR, Article 28: Processor
items.locator: Art. 28(3)(h); read with Art. 28(1)
items.quote: allow for and contribute to audits, including inspections, conducted by the controller or another auditor mandated by the controller
items.why: The one audit right that general UK law writes into supplier contracts. Where a supplier processes personal data on the buyer's behalf, the contract must require it to make available the information needed to show compliance and to allow audits and inspections by the buyer or its auditor. Applies only where personal data is processed and the supplier is a processor, so it does not reach every AI purchase. Current revised text on legislation.gov.uk.

items.title: FCA Handbook, SYSC 8.1: General outsourcing requirements
items.locator: SYSC 8.1.8R(9); also 8.1.6R (firm remains fully responsible), 8.1.7R (due skill, care and diligence), 8.1.8R(2), (6), (7) and (12) (performance review, disclosure of material developments, termination, continuity). Provisions shown as dated 23/10/2025
items.quote: must have effective access to data related to the outsourced activities, as well as to the business premises of the service provider
items.why: A binding regulator rule, not guidance. A firm that outsources critical or important functions must assess the supplier's performance on an ongoing basis, be told of material developments, be able to terminate, keep continuity on exit, and have access for itself and its auditors to the supplier's data and premises. Sector-specific: these rules bind 'common platform firms' as the Handbook defines them, and SYSC 8.1.1AG tells other firms to treat the main outsourcing rule as guidance; it covers outsourcing of critical or important functions, not every purchase. Not written for AI.

items.title: AI Act, Article 25: Responsibilities along the AI value chain (AI Act Service Desk copy)
items.locator: Article 25(4), marked AMENDED; 'About this text' notice
items.quote: shall, by written agreement, specify the necessary information, capabilities, technical access and other assistance based on the generally acknowledged state of the art
items.why: The Commission's own copy, not the Official Journal; it says the text follows the EUR-Lex consolidated version of the AI Act as at 27 July 2026 and marks Digital Omnibus changes. The provider of a high-risk system and any third party supplying a model, tool, component or service built into it must set out in a written agreement the information and technical access the provider needs to comply. A duty between provider and upstream supplier, not on a deployer; relevant only to organisations within the Act's reach, and the high-risk rules are not yet in application.

items.title: AI tools in recruitment: audit outcomes report
items.locator: Executive summary, pp.3-4; 'Third party relationships' section, p.47 onwards (recommendations for recruiters)
items.quote: Some had attempted to pass all responsibility for compliance to recruiters using their tool.
items.why: A regulator's audit finding on what suppliers actually do. In consensual audits of AI recruitment tool providers the regulator found providers wrongly calling themselves processors, vague contracts that left the buying recruiter 'in the dark', and attempts to pass all responsibility to the buyer. It recommends that buyers obtain evidence of controls before purchase and run compliance checks through the life of the contract. Recruitment tools only; data protection only; the number of organisations audited is small.

items.title: Government's approach to technology suppliers: addressing the challenges (HC 543, Session 2024-25)
items.locator: Summary, key finding citing paragraphs 2.8, 2.11, 2.13 and 2.15 (p.9); paragraphs 2.13-2.15 ('Being an intelligent client')
items.quote: departments dedicate substantial resources to putting a contract in place but insufficient attention and resources to managing the contract after award
items.why: The public auditor's finding on through-life supplier management: effort goes into letting a technology contract and too little into managing it afterwards, and government 'struggles to act as an intelligent client'. Estimates at least £14 billion a year of government digital procurement. About digital and technology suppliers in central government generally; AI is mentioned only as part of a market dominated by very large suppliers. Not a study of AI procurement.

items.title: R (Bridges) v Chief Constable of South Wales Police [2020] EWCA Civ 1058
items.publisher: Court of Appeal (Civil Division), published by The National Archives
items.locator: Paragraph 199 (Ground 5, public sector equality duty); paragraphs 200-201
items.quote: for reasons of commercial confidentiality, the manufacturer is not prepared to divulge the details so that it could be tested
items.why: A court finding on buying AI without checking it. The police force had never satisfied itself, directly or through independent verification, that bought-in facial recognition software was free of unacceptable race or sex bias; the supplier would not release details of its training data. The court held that a supplier's commercial confidentiality does not let a public authority discharge its own non-delegable equality duty. Binding on public authorities under the Equality Act 2010 section 149; it is not a ruling about private-sector buyers.

items.title: Understanding accountability in algorithmic supply chains
items.publisher: Jennifer Cobbe, Michael Veale and Jatinder Singh (arXiv; ACM FAccT 2023)
items.locator: Abstract (arXiv:2304.14749v2)
items.quote: challenges for allocating accountability stemming from distributed responsibility for systems between actors, limited visibility due to the accountability horizon
items.why: Peer-reviewed conference paper, read on the authors' arXiv copy. Argues that AI is increasingly delivered through chains of suppliers linked by data flows, and that this spreads responsibility between actors and limits how far any one of them, the deploying organisation included, can see along the chain. Conceptual and legal analysis, not an empirical study; it explains why a buyer's due diligence cannot stop at the immediate vendor.

items.title: Dislocated Accountabilities in the AI Supply Chain: Modularity and Developers' Notions of Responsibility
items.publisher: David Gray Widder and Dawn Nafus (arXiv; Big Data & Society 10(1), 2023)
items.locator: Abstract (arXiv:2209.09780v3)
items.quote: our participants often did not see the questions posed in responsible artificial intelligence guidelines to be within their agency, capability, or responsibility to address
items.why: Empirical evidence from the supplier side. In interviews with 27 AI engineers, participants commonly treated questions of harm as the job of the previous or next party in the supply chain. Shows why a buyer cannot assume the vendor has done the checking. Small qualitative sample; where the engineers worked is not stated in the abstract. Read on the authors' arXiv copy of a journal article.

items.title: Buying AI: Is the public sector equipped to procure technology in the public interest?
items.locator: Executive summary ('A review of guidance, legislation and policy documents'); 'Document analysis'
items.quote: local government does not have access to a clear or comprehensive account of how to procure AI in the public interest
items.why: A UK documentary review of 16 pieces of guidance, legislation and policy on procuring AI and data-driven systems. Finds the guidance fragmented and leaves local authorities to interpret fairness, transparency and supplier responsibilities for themselves. An independent research institute's report, not peer reviewed; the documents reviewed were all published under the 2010-24 government, so the 2025 AI Playbook and the Procurement Act's commencement post-date it.

items.title: Updated EU AI model contractual clauses (MCC-AI)
items.locator: Description; file list (commentary, high-risk version, light version)
items.quote: a full version for high-risk AI, aligned with the EU AI Act adopted on 13 June 2024
items.why: Ready-made contract terms for buying AI: a full set for high-risk systems, a lighter set for other AI, and a commentary on how to use them. Published by a community of practice of public buyers hosted by the Commission; voluntary, and drafted for EU law and public procurement. Only the landing page was read in this pass, not the clauses themselves. Useful as a starting point for the documentation, audit and change-notification terms the criterion's top level asks for.
